query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor addition of a ductile BCC-forming element (e.g., Nb) to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy will promote the in‐situ formation of nanoscale, coherent Nb‐rich precipitates along grain boundaries. These precipitates are expected to bridge cracks and toughen the material without significantly perturbing the magnetostructural transition that gives rise to the large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy that exhibits large caloric effects under applied field and pressure but suffers from poor integrity with crack propagation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small (e.g., 2–5 at.%) Nb addition during alloy synthesis to encourage a controlled precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: Under operational conditions similar to the original system – namely, exposure to applied magnetic and pressure fields and temperatures where the caloric response is active.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, ductile Nb‐rich precipitates forming at or near grain boundaries to inhibit or arrest crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The Nb addition is anticipated to induce a minor change in the alloy’s phase equilibria such that coherent precipitates form; these precipitates improve toughness and compressive strength by arresting crack initiation and propagation while the dominant phase transition that drives the caloric effect remains largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in mechanical integrity (e.g., an increase in compressive strength to levels modestly higher than the best reported composites, such as above 220 MPa) and enhanced crack resistance, with the caloric response (magnitude of adiabatic temperature or entropy change) remaining within approximately 10% of the original performance.
generation.baseline: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits high caloric response but with low mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.boundary: The effects are hypothesized to hold under field-driven and pressure-driven operation at temperatures and loading regimes where the caloric effect is activated (as per the original material’s operating window). Extreme deviations in processing conditions or field strengths might alter the behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Nb required to achieve an optimal precipitate size and distribution, as well as the full impact of these precipitates on the caloric transition, remains to be determined. There is a risk that even minor compositional changes could partially alter the transition driving the caloric effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with identical processing: a control group of the base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and an experimental group with a 2–5 at.% Nb addition. Subject both groups to the same heat treatments and then evaluate mechanical integrity using compressive strength and crack propagation tests as well as measuring the caloric response (e.g., adiabatic temperature change and isothermal entropy change) under identical applied-field and pressure-field conditions.
measurements: Crack initiation and propagation via microstructural analysis
Caloric effect metrics (adiabatic temperature change, isothermal entropy change)
Phase and precipitate analysis via microscopy and diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Nb-added samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., compressive strength increase and reduced crack formation) relative to the control while maintaining a caloric response within ±10% of that measured in the unmodified alloy.
